title: The qubit
summary: Meet the quantum bit and the state vector that describes its possible measurement outcomes.
content:
A classical bit is recorded as either 0 or 1. A qubit is a physical quantum system whose state can be described by amplitudes for the basis states |0> and |1>. Those amplitudes predict measurement probabilities; they are not ordinary probabilities themselves.

A qubit might be encoded in an atom, a photon, or a superconducting circuit. The mathematical model is shared, but real devices differ in how they control, measure, and protect their qubits.

title: Basis states & Dirac notation
summary: Read ket notation and understand the computational basis used to describe qubit states.
content:
The symbols |0> and |1> are kets: compact labels for two orthogonal basis states. A single-qubit state can be written as alpha|0> + beta|1>, where alpha and beta are complex amplitudes and their squared magnitudes sum to one.

For several qubits, basis labels combine into bit strings such as |00>, |01>, |10>, and |11>. Keeping the basis order consistent is essential when interpreting a circuit or a simulator's output.

title: Superposition
summary: Understand how amplitudes combine to describe a qubit before measurement.
content:
A superposition is a coherent combination of basis states. For example, the Hadamard gate maps |0> to (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2), so a computational-basis measurement returns either result with equal probability.

It is misleading to picture a qubit as a hidden classical bit that is simply both values at once. The relative amplitudes and phases matter because later operations can make alternatives reinforce or cancel through interference.

title: Measurement & the Born rule
summary: Connect quantum amplitudes to observed probabilities and understand measurement collapse.
content:
When a state is measured in a chosen basis, the Born rule says that the probability of each outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude. A state with equal amplitudes for |0> and |1> therefore produces a balanced distribution over many repeated shots.

A single measurement gives one outcome, not the full probability distribution. Repeating the same preparation and measurement lets an experiment estimate that distribution. Measurement in another basis requires changing the circuit before reading the result.

title: Quantum interference
summary: See how phase-sensitive amplitudes reinforce or cancel in a quantum circuit.
content:
Quantum alternatives carry amplitudes with phase. When two paths lead to the same result, their amplitudes combine before probabilities are calculated. Depending on their relative phase, the paths can reinforce one another or partially cancel.

A useful circuit exercise is to apply H twice to |0>. The first H creates two amplitudes; the second recombines them so the state returns to |0>. The intermediate superposition is real, but the final interference determines what is measured.

title: Phase & the Bloch sphere
summary: Visualize a pure single-qubit state and distinguish global from relative phase.
content:
The Bloch sphere maps pure single-qubit states to points on a sphere. The north and south poles represent |0> and |1>; other points encode superpositions with different relative amplitudes and phases. Rotations around sphere axes correspond to common single-qubit operations.

Multiplying every amplitude by the same global phase does not change measurement predictions. Changing the relative phase between basis components can change interference and is physically observable. The sphere is a visualization of a state, not a picture of a tiny spinning object.

title: Quantum gates & unitaries
summary: Learn why ideal quantum gates are reversible unitary transformations.
content:
A quantum gate transforms a state vector. In an ideal circuit, the transformation is unitary, which preserves total probability and is reversible. A gate can change basis-state amplitudes and phases without directly reading the state.

Gates are applied in sequence to build a circuit. A measurement is different: it produces a classical outcome and changes what can be predicted about the remaining quantum state. Hardware may only provide a particular native gate set, so circuits are often rewritten into supported operations.

title: Pauli X, Y & Z gates
summary: Compare bit flips, phase flips, and the three Pauli operators.
content:
The Pauli X gate swaps |0> and |1>, acting like a classical NOT on basis states. The Z gate leaves |0> unchanged and flips the sign of the |1> amplitude, changing phase rather than the computational-basis value. Y combines the two kinds of action with complex phase factors.

These operators are also observables used to describe measurements and physical quantities. Testing each gate on |0>, |1>, and a superposition makes the difference between bit value and phase easier to see.

title: The Hadamard gate
summary: Use H to change between computational basis states and balanced superpositions.
content:
The Hadamard gate maps |0> to an equal positive superposition and |1> to an equal superposition with a relative minus sign. It is its own inverse, so applying H twice returns the original state.

The sign difference is invisible to a direct measurement in the computational basis but becomes important after another operation. That makes H a compact way to study basis changes and interference in a simulator or on a quantum device.

title: Phase, S, T & rotation gates
summary: Explore gates that rotate a qubit's phase and why non-Clifford rotations matter.
content:
Phase gates leave |0> unchanged and multiply |1> by a phase factor. The S and T gates are common fixed rotations around the Z axis of the Bloch sphere; parameterized RZ, RX, and RY gates allow a chosen rotation angle.

A phase operation can appear to do nothing when the qubit is exactly |0> or |1>, yet change the result after a basis change. Non-Clifford gates such as T also matter in fault-tolerant computing because they extend circuits beyond the efficiently simulable Clifford family.

title: Quantum circuits
summary: Read circuit wires, operations, circuit depth, and the role of measurement.
content:
A quantum circuit is an ordered description of operations on qubits. Wires track qubits through time; gates are operations, and measurement maps selected quantum information to classical bits. Independent gates can sometimes share a circuit layer, while dependent operations must remain ordered.

Circuit depth counts sequential layers rather than total gate count. On real hardware, reducing depth can help limit accumulated noise. Drawing a circuit and reading its code are two views of the same executable description.

title: Controlled gates & CNOT
summary: Understand conditional two-qubit operations and their control-target structure.
content:
A controlled gate applies an operation to a target when a control qubit is in a specified state. CNOT, often written CX, flips its target if the control is |1> and otherwise leaves it alone. It is a two-qubit unitary operation.

The order of control and target matters. Applying H to a control and then CNOT can create entanglement, while applying CNOT to computational-basis inputs may simply permute bit strings. Inspect both the circuit and resulting state to understand the operation.

title: Entanglement & Bell states
summary: Explore joint states whose correlations cannot be described as independent qubits.
content:
A two-qubit state is entangled when it cannot be factored into separate states for each qubit. A Bell state such as (|00> + |11>)/sqrt(2) gives perfectly correlated computational-basis measurements even though neither qubit alone has a definite result.

Entanglement is a resource used in teleportation, communication, and algorithms. It does not allow faster-than-light messaging: local measurement outcomes are random, and comparing correlations still requires classical communication.

title: The no-cloning theorem
summary: Learn why an unknown quantum state cannot be perfectly copied.
content:
No-cloning is a consequence of linear quantum evolution: there is no single physical operation that copies every possible unknown state exactly. Basis states can be copied into correlated states with gates such as CNOT, but that does not create a universal copier for arbitrary superpositions.

This limitation is not a software restriction. It shapes quantum communication and security, and it is one reason quantum information protocols behave differently from copying classical data.

title: Quantum noise & decoherence
summary: See how imperfect gates and the environment change circuit outcomes.
content:
Real quantum processors are affected by imperfect operations, readout errors, and interactions with their environment. Decoherence describes the loss of useful phase relationships, while noise models represent errors such as bit flips, phase flips, or depolarization.

A noiseless simulator predicts ideal behavior. A noisy simulation applies an explicit error model and can help compare ideal and realistic distributions. Noise is device- and operation-dependent, so a simulation model should be treated as an approximation rather than a guarantee about hardware.

title: Density matrices & mixed states
summary: Represent uncertainty and noisy quantum states with density operators.
content:
A state vector describes a pure state with a definite preparation. A density matrix can represent pure states as well as statistical mixtures and reduced states of subsystems. Its diagonal entries encode basis measurement probabilities, while off-diagonal terms carry coherence information.

Tracing out part of an entangled system can leave the remaining qubit in a mixed state even when the full joint system is pure. Density matrices are therefore useful for reasoning about noise, partial information, and open quantum systems.

title: Quantum simulation & shots
summary: Compare exact state simulation with repeated circuit sampling and noisy runs.
content:
An exact statevector simulator computes the ideal amplitudes for a circuit. A shot-based run samples measurement outcomes from the resulting distribution, so finite-shot counts vary between runs. More shots generally improve estimates but require more execution time.

Noisy simulation adds modeled errors to approximate a device. Histograms make distributions easier to inspect, but the backend and settings matter: distinguish exact probabilities, sampled counts, and hardware measurements when interpreting a plot.

title: Hardware connectivity & transpilation
summary: Learn why logical circuits are mapped and optimized for a device's native gates.
content:
A circuit can describe logical operations that a particular processor cannot perform directly. Transpilation rewrites and routes those operations into a device-supported gate set while respecting which qubits can interact.

Routing may add swaps, increasing depth and exposure to noise. Two equivalent logical circuits can therefore have different hardware costs. Inspecting a transpiled circuit helps connect abstract algorithms to real processor constraints.

title: Quantum error correction & stabilizers
summary: Understand how logical information is protected using encoded states and syndrome checks.
content:
Quantum error correction encodes one logical qubit across multiple physical qubits. Carefully chosen parity-like checks reveal information about errors without directly measuring and destroying the encoded logical state. The resulting pattern is called an error syndrome.

Stabilizer codes describe many useful codes using commuting Pauli checks. Error correction requires extra qubits and operations, so practical fault tolerance depends on hardware quality, code design, and repeated correction cycles.

title: Quantum teleportation
summary: Transfer an unknown quantum state using entanglement, measurement, and classical messages.
content:
Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown state using a shared entangled pair, a joint measurement, and two classical bits. The sender's original state is consumed by the measurement; the protocol does not copy it or send matter across space.

The receiver applies a correction determined by the classical message and recovers the original state. Building the protocol as a circuit demonstrates how entanglement and classical communication work together.

title: Quantum key distribution
summary: Use quantum measurement statistics to detect interference during key exchange.
content:
Quantum key distribution protocols let participants establish correlated key bits and use public discussion to estimate whether a transmission was disturbed. In the BB84 example, randomly chosen preparation and measurement bases make interception detectable in the observed error rate.

The protocol distributes key material; it does not encrypt messages by itself. Practical security also depends on authenticated classical communication and implementation details of the devices.

title: Oracles & the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
summary: See how phase kickback and interference reveal a global property of a function.
content:
An oracle is a circuit component that encodes a problem function into a reversible quantum operation. The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm uses an oracle and interference to determine whether a promised function is constant or balanced with one ideal query.

The speedup is for a carefully defined query model, not a claim that every task becomes faster on a quantum computer. Small oracle circuits are a good way to learn phase kickback, ancillas, and algorithm assumptions.

title: Grover's search algorithm
summary: Amplify the amplitude of marked answers in an unstructured search problem.
content:
Grover's algorithm alternates an oracle that marks solutions with a diffusion operation that reflects amplitudes. Repeating this process increases the probability of measuring a marked item. For an unstructured search over N possibilities, the query count scales roughly as sqrt(N).

The number of iterations matters: too many can rotate amplitudes past the optimum. The algorithm offers a quadratic query improvement, not an exponential advantage, and the cost of implementing the oracle must be included in a fair comparison.

title: Quantum Fourier transform
summary: Use controlled phase rotations and Hadamards to transform amplitudes between bases.
content:
The quantum Fourier transform is the unitary analogue of a discrete Fourier transform on amplitudes. It can be built from Hadamard gates and controlled phase rotations, with swaps to arrange output order.

The transform is a key component in phase estimation and Shor's algorithm. Its compact circuit does not automatically provide a speedup for every Fourier task; the benefit depends on how the transformed quantum state is used and measured.

title: Shor's factoring algorithm
summary: Connect period finding and the quantum Fourier transform to integer factoring.
content:
Shor's algorithm reduces factoring to finding the period of a modular arithmetic function. Quantum phase estimation and the Fourier transform help extract information about that period; classical post-processing then turns a useful period into factors.

The complete algorithm has important resource requirements. Small demonstrations illustrate the mathematics, but today's noisy devices cannot factor cryptographically large integers with this method. Separating the quantum subroutine from classical processing clarifies where the algorithm's advantage arises.

title: Variational quantum eigensolver
summary: Combine parameterized circuits and classical optimization to estimate low-energy states.
content:
The variational quantum eigensolver prepares a parameterized trial state, measures terms of a problem Hamiltonian, and uses a classical optimizer to update circuit parameters. Repeating this hybrid loop aims to lower the estimated energy.

VQE is useful as a framework for studying quantum chemistry and optimization, but success depends on the ansatz, noise, measurement cost, and optimization landscape. The variational principle gives an upper bound on the ground-state energy when its assumptions are met.

title: QAOA & quantum optimization
summary: Encode a discrete optimization problem into alternating parameterized circuit layers.
content:
The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm encodes an objective as a cost Hamiltonian and alternates it with a mixing operation. Circuit angles are optimized in a classical loop, and measurements provide candidate solutions.

QAOA is a hybrid algorithm family, not a guarantee of better optimization. Problem encoding, circuit depth, shot noise, and classical optimization all affect performance. Small Max-Cut examples make its cost and mixer layers easy to inspect.

title: Quantum walks
summary: Compare classical random walks with interference-driven evolution on a graph.
content:
A classical random walk moves between graph nodes according to transition probabilities. A quantum walk evolves amplitudes over nodes, often with a coin degree of freedom; interference can reshape how probability spreads through the graph.

Quantum walks appear in algorithm design and physical models. The exact construction can be discrete- or continuous-time, so it is important to state the walk model before comparing its behavior with a classical process.

title: Random circuit sampling
summary: Study complex output distributions produced by randomly structured quantum circuits.
content:
Random circuit sampling applies layers of selected gates to many qubits and samples the resulting output bit strings. The distributions can be difficult for classical methods to predict as circuit width and depth grow, making this a useful benchmarking problem.

A sampling benchmark is not automatically a practical application. Results depend on circuit design, device fidelity, and the classical comparison method. It connects circuit architecture, calibration, noise, and statistical validation.
